questions.prompt: A script awaits a single `agent()` call directly at the top — a prerequisite that must succeed before the fan-out. You stop that agent mid-run from `/workflows`. What happens to the run?
options: It ends with the error, because an awaited agent that is lost is not a slot in a fan-out
It carries on, with `null` in the place of that agent's result
It restarts the agent; stopping counts as a stall
It pauses until you resume, then continues from the next step
questions.explanation: The failure behaviour depends on *where the call sits*, not on which combinator is nearby: inside `parallel()` or `pipeline()` the run continues with `null` in the slot, but a directly awaited call ends the run with the error. The `null` answer is tempting because it is the documented behaviour one line lower in the script — it belongs to fan-out members. A manual stop is not a stall, so no automatic restart follows; and the runtime does not quietly continue past a load-bearing failure.

questions.prompt: A `pipeline()` over 412 files returned 412 entries, 16 of them `null`. A colleague asks which files failed. What do you do?
options: Match each `null`'s index back to the input list, and add `label` so the next run names them for you
Read the error message stored on each `null` entry
Count the `null`s and re-run the whole pipeline, since you cannot tell which files they were
Sort the array so the `null`s group together, then re-run those positions
questions.explanation: A `null` is a placeholder that keeps its position in the array, so its index still points at the file that produced it — and adding a `label` to each `agent()` call makes the mapping readable in `/workflows` next time. The error-message answer is the natural instinct and is wrong: the runtime substitutes a bare `null` in place of the agent's result, and any reason for the loss is reported around the run rather than attached to the slot. Re-running everything or reordering the array discards the positional information that was the only thing telling you which files failed.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `parallel()` and `pipeline()` is actually supported by the documentation?
options: Both wait for all of their agents, and neither returns as soon as one finishes
`pipeline()` bounds concurrency while `parallel()` starts every task at once
`pipeline()` runs items one after another while `parallel()` runs them concurrently
`parallel()` returns results as agents finish, in completion order
questions.explanation: The docs describe `parallel()` as running a set of tasks at the same time and waiting for all of them, and `pipeline()` as running one agent per item; both are subject to the same runtime concurrency cap. Everything else here is a plausible invention. The two 'one is parallel and one is not' answers are the most seductive, because the names imply a scheduling difference the docs never draw, and the failure-handling section applies identically to both. Completion-order results are the opposite of the documented behaviour and are the subject of Lesson 80.

questions.prompt: An audit agent can legitimately find nothing and report an empty result. You must be able to tell that apart from an agent that never came back. What do you build?
options: Give the agent a `schema` so 'found nothing' is a well-formed empty list, and check for `null` separately as 'the agent was lost'
Treat an empty string and a `null` as the same failure, since both mean no finding
Add `.filter(Boolean)` so the empty ones drop out and only real findings remain
Ask a second verifier agent to decide whether the first one really ran
questions.explanation: A well-formed empty result and a `null` slot are different facts, and conflating them is the bug from the opening story. Passing a `schema` makes the first one structured — the docs describe `agent()` returning validated JSON against the shape, and failing the call after bounded retries when it cannot. The merge-both-into-failure answer destroys exactly the distinction you need. `.filter(Boolean)` removes the evidence and shifts every later slot, and a verifier cannot see an agent that never returned.

questions.prompt: A list of 5,000 files is passed to one `pipeline()` call. What does the runtime do?
options: Rejects the call with an error, rather than quietly running part of the list
Runs the first 4,096 and reports the count it skipped
Splits the list into two batches automatically and runs both
Runs all 5,000, just more slowly than usual
questions.explanation: There is a hard cap on the number of items in a single `parallel()` or `pipeline()` call, and the runtime rejects a longer list with an error. The docs give the reason explicitly: a silent cap would drop part of the workload without telling the script. That makes the truncation answer the most dangerous wrong one — it assumes the failure mode is data loss the script can detect, when the actual failure is a loud rejection. Automatic batching and running-anyway belong to neither behaviour.
